records.sourceFile: Stress Relaxation and Targeted    Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy.pdf

paper.citation: Baar K. Stress relaxation and targeted nutrition to treat patellar tendinopathy. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2018 (accepted manuscript; volume and pages not printed).
paper.abstract: Describes the rehabilitation of a professional basketball player with MRI-confirmed central core patellar tendinopathy, treated with gelatin ingestion and heavy isometric loading over 18 months. MRI improved, pain decreased, and performance improved; the author concludes the combined program can improve clinical outcomes in elite athletes.
paper.tldr: In one elite basketball player, an 18-month program of isometric stress-relaxation loading with pre-load gelatin was followed by normalized MRI, less pain and large strength gains. This is a single uncontrolled case that supports trying the approach, not proving it works.
paper.methods: Single-case study of one professional male basketball player (21 years old at first MRI). Twice-weekly mid-range isometric holds of 10 to 30 seconds at more than 80% 1RM (leg extension, leg press, Spanish squat), with 15 g gelatin and about 225 mg vitamin C taken one hour before loading. Follow-up MRIs were taken 15 months after the initial scan (about 12 months into the program) and 6 months later (about 18 months into the program), with the final images judged by a blinded orthopedic surgeon; the initial MRI was done on a different machine, and isometric strength was measured on an isokinetic dynamometer. Compliance was reported above 95% in season.
paper.findings: MRI reactivity at the inferior pole of the patella decreased progressively and the surgeon declared the tendon normal at the final scan. The proximal tendon diameter fell from 10.8 mm to 8.16 mm (about 25%) and the mid-tendon diameter rose from 5.74 mm to 6.29 mm. Self-reported pain and tenderness decreased, and single-leg isometric strength increased by 196% (hamstring), 156% (leg extension) and 187.5% (leg press) across the program. Body mass fell 2.5 kg and lean mass fell slightly (75.6 kg to 74.7 kg) while body fat fell from 8.4% to 5.9%.
paper.limitations: With one athlete and no control group, the cause of the change cannot be isolated from the gelatin, the loading, or natural healing. The abstract states that performance improved, but apart from isometric strength the results report no performance measure, so on-court performance claims are not supported by data in the text. Pain was self-reported, and the baseline MRI was taken on a different scanner from the follow-ups. Collagen synthesis was not measured, and the team-wide injury reduction was not quantified.
paper.practicalImplications: For an elite athlete with chronic central core patellar tendinopathy, the author's program (progressive heavy isometric holds twice weekly plus 15 g gelatin with vitamin C an hour before loading) was followed by normal-appearing MRI and less pain in one case. Staff can consider it as one part of a supervised rehab plan, with MRI and pain tracked over time.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The paper gives a loading and nutrition template for keeping a tendon-affected athlete in strength work. It shows strength gains in one player across the program, but it does not show that the approach improves performance on court.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The player kept competing during the program (more than 50 games per season, averaging more than 20 minutes) and was pain free at the final scan while playing more than 25 minutes a game, but the paper does not report when he returned to play or compare recovery time with other treatment. It cannot be used to set a return-to-play timeline or to guarantee tendon recovery in other athletes.

records.sourceFile: Surgically treated pectoralis major tears impact the play and performance of National Football League athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Farooq H, Garbis NG, Moossighi R, Lam R, Cho E, Salazar DH. Surgically Treated Pectoralis Major Tears Impact the Play and Performance of National Football League Athletes. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2022:e1-e6.
paper.abstract: This descriptive epidemiologic study reviewed NFL players with surgically treated pectoralis major tears to assess return-to-play rate and changes in performance. Of 24 players, 20 (83%) returned to play, and performance scores fell significantly across the cohort, but not after stratifying by position or draft round.
paper.tldr: Most NFL players (20 of 24) with surgically repaired pectoralis major tears returned to play, after a mean of about 302 days. Average performance scores fell after return, but the drop was not significant within position or draft-round groups.
paper.methods: A descriptive epidemiologic study of NFL players from 1933 to 2013, using a public transactions archive to find pectoralis major tears that were treated surgically. Two blinded investigators confirmed the cases, and performance scores based on a previously published calculation were compared before and after injury using paired-samples t tests.
paper.findings: Twenty-four players with surgically repaired tears were included, and 20 (83%) returned to play, with a mean return-to-play period of 302 days (SD 128). Across the 20 players, the mean performance score fell from 299.26 to 127.94 (difference 171.33, 95% CI 15.74 to 326.91, P = .033). The decrease was not significant in the defensive (P = .064), offensive (P = .366), round 1 or 2 (P = .075) or round 3 or later (P = .264) subgroups. No player returned in the same season as injury, and all four players who did not return played defensive positions.
paper.limitations: The authors note low incidence and small numbers, which limit statistical power, and that the public database gives little information on tear severity, mechanism, concomitant injuries or operative technique. Findings may not apply to collegiate, high school or recreational athletes, and some tears may have been missed. The study has no control group and no adjustment for confounders.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use these figures to set realistic expectations for NFL players after surgical repair of a pectoralis major tear, with about 83% returning and a mean of about 10 months away. The study does not identify factors that predict an individual's outcome.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the study shows a group-level drop in performance score after return, but the drop was not significant within position or draft-round groups. It does not provide training or load guidance for rebuilding performance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the study supports expecting most NFL players to return after surgical repair, with a mean of 302 days to play. It cannot be used for an individual clearance decision, because it has no measure of injury severity, operative technique or functional testing criteria.

paper.citation: Mitchell A, Holding C. The management of a professional footballer recovering from a surgical repair of the proximal adductor longus tendon through a return-to-performance pathway. A case report. Research in Sports Medicine. 2024.
paper.abstract: A 23-year-old professional footballer had a rupture of the proximal adductor longus tendon, was treated with surgical reattachment, and completed an eleven-phase return-to-performance pathway that combined clinical, performance and sport-specific criteria. The player returned to competitive play 12 weeks after surgery. The authors describe the shared decision-making process used by the interdisciplinary team.
paper.tldr: A single professional footballer returned to competitive play at 12 weeks after surgical adductor longus reattachment using a phase-gated, criteria-based pathway. The case shows how the criteria were sequenced, but it cannot show what typical recovery looks like.
paper.methods: Single-case clinical report. The player was managed through three gym phases and six grass phases, with progression gated by pain (2/10 or less), a confidence rating (80% or more), and objective measures such as adductor squeeze, hip range of motion, hop tests, force plate jumps, and GPS-monitored running loads.
paper.findings: At weeks 6.5 to 7, adductor squeeze and hip range of motion were within 10% of pre-injury values, while plyometric and hop measures needed only 80% of pre-injury values, and running began at week 7. In grass phase 3 he reached 94% of peak speed, 96% of peak acceleration intensity and 84% of peak deceleration intensity. He completed a 45-minute U23 match at 12 weeks and joined the regular match schedule from week 14.
paper.limitations: One player with no comparison group, so the pathway's effect cannot be separated from the player's own recovery. The abstract states return to competitive play at 12 weeks, while the body describes a U23 match at 12 weeks and full match play from week 14. Figure 2 and Table 1 values are not reproduced in the extracted text, and the adductor strength thresholds were taken from earlier published studies rather than tested here.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff managing a surgical adductor longus repair can use this phase structure as a worked example of gating progression on pain, confidence and objective profiling. The case does not justify fixed return dates; the timeline came from one player's responses at each gate.
paper.athleteDev: The pathway sequenced gym-based profiling (hop battery, force plate jumps, adductor and abductor strength) alongside GPS-limited running, acceleration and kicking progressions. Kicking distance rose from 2 m to 10 m in grass phase 1 and to 40 m in grass phase 2, alongside high-speed running and agility work.
paper.rtp: This case describes one professional footballer's return after surgical adductor longus reattachment, with a U23 match at 12 weeks and full match play from week 14. It cannot establish expected return times for other players, other repair types, or other clubs, and it cannot show that the pathway caused the outcome.

records.sourceFile: The British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification grading system as a predictor of return to play following hamstrings injury in professional soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Tears C, Rae G, Hide G, Sinha R, Franklin J, Brand P, et al. The British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification grading system as a predictor of return to play following hamstrings injury in professional football players. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2022.
paper.abstract: The authors compared the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC) grade, oedema length and cross-sectional area on MRI with return to play after primary hamstring strain in 39 professional footballers. BAMIC grade had a weak but significant correlation with return to play, and BAMIC and Peetron's grading agreed only slightly.
paper.tldr: The BAMIC grade on MRI is weakly linked to how long a professional footballer takes to return to play after a hamstring strain. It agrees only slightly with Peetron's grading, so it should be one input among several.
paper.methods: Retrospective cohort at one professional English club, 2010 to 2019, with male players who had an MRI within 7 days of a primary hamstring strain. Two musculoskeletal radiologists graded the scans, and Pearson correlations and multiple regression were used to relate the grades and MRI measures to return to play, with kappa for agreement between the two grading systems.
paper.findings: Among 39 injuries, BAMIC grade correlated weakly with return to play (r = 0.32, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.58, p = 0.05). Oedema length was weakly correlated (r = 0.3, p = 0.06) and cross-sectional area was not (r = 0.02, p = 0.91). The multiple regression explained 16% of the variance in return to play, and kappa for BAMIC against Peetron's was 0.21 (95% CI 0 to 0.42).
paper.limitations: Only one club was studied, so the sample is small and the regression results are unstable. The authors acknowledge that the lack of significance for cross-sectional area and oedema length may reflect sample size, and call for larger replication. The retrospective design relies on historical MRI and medical records. The multiple regression model was not statistically significant (F p = 0.1), and the single-predictor BAMIC model explained only 10% of the variance, so the 16% figure is the multivariable model and it is not a significant fit.
paper.practicalImplications: Grade hamstring strains with BAMIC alongside clinical findings and use the grade as a rough guide to return to play timing. Do not rely on oedema length or cross-sectional area as predictors, and expect weak prediction for individual players.
paper.athleteDev: Not applicable. The paper studies injured players' return to play after a hamstring strain and does not address performance training.
paper.rtp: Use BAMIC grading from the first MRI, within 7 days of onset, as one input to return-to-play planning for hamstring strains in professional football. The grade has only weak predictive value, so it should not be used alone to set a return date.

records.sourceFile: The Impact of Daylight Exposure on Injured Athletes - Implications for Rehabilitation.pdf

paper.citation: Niering M, Seifert J. The Impact of Daylight Exposure on Injured Athletes: Implications for Rehabilitation. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2024.
paper.abstract: During injury rehabilitation and return to competition, factors such as psychological parameters, sleep quality and vitamin D levels affect outcomes. The authors review existing research and theory on daylight effects on athletes in rehabilitation, organised into sun-induced vitamin D synthesis, cognitive-behavioural processes, the circadian mechanism and visual processing of light. They propose a low-cost artificial daylight intervention that could accompany injury therapy in clinics and clubs.
paper.tldr: Daylight may be a cheap add-on to injury rehabilitation, but no study has tested it in injured athletes. The supporting evidence comes from healthy or non-athlete samples, small studies and animal work, so treat the proposed light timing as a hypothesis to trial.
paper.methods: Narrative review. PubMed, PsycINFO and Google Scholar were searched for records from 1 January 1960 to 20 October 2023, in German or English, using combined terms for daylight, sunlight or light with sports injury and injury rehabilitation terms. No criteria on study design, population or quality were applied. Reference lists of included studies were searched manually.
paper.findings: No study has examined daylight exposure directly on the prevalence or rehabilitation of sports injuries. Related findings include: in high-performance athletes, 10 days of winter sunlight nearly matched a 6-week regimen of 6000 IU/day vitamin D for raising serum 25(OH)D and testosterone (Michalczyk et al. 2020); in two groups of ten male athletes, light exposure timed to the circadian rhythm had large effects on sleep duration after long-haul travel compared with no intervention, with small to moderate effects on jump and sprint measures (Fowler et al. 2021); and in non-athletes, artificial sunlight and vitamin D supplementation both raised 25(OH)D without a change in athletic performance (Carswell et al. 2018).
paper.limitations: Not a systematic search, and no quality appraisal of included studies. Most evidence comes from non-athletes, animal models or very small samples (the cited studies of daylight and sleep in clinical populations had one to 20 participants). The authors note that most vitamin D and testosterone work has been done in males, so no conclusions can be drawn for females. The Table 1 effects come from studies that were not of injured athletes in rehabilitation, and the proposed protocol has not been evaluated.
paper.practicalImplications: Daylight could be a low-cost adjunct, but the evidence is indirect. If it is tried, the authors propose timing sessions by chronotype (morning types 2 to 4 hours after waking, evening types after sunset, with sessions finished about three hours before bed), a dawn simulation device for 30 minutes before waking, a daylight LED for 30 minutes after waking, and group sessions. These are proposals and should be tracked for sleep, mood and rehabilitation progress.
paper.athleteDev: Light timing is worth a small pilot rather than adoption as a performance tool. Evidence for better sleep and jump or sprint measures after circadian-timed light comes from one small study of male athletes, and vitamin D findings differed between athletes and non-athletes, so keep it alongside routine sleep and nutrition care and record sleep and performance if it is trialled.
paper.rtp: It cannot show that daylight or light therapy shortens rehabilitation or speeds return to competition. The authors' suggestion that the approach could reduce injury duration is a hypothesis, not a finding of the review.
